subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 16 periods = 640 minutes
Total: 16 periods · 10h 40min

periods.activity_title: From a Dot to a Line: Building Blocks of Geometry

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 2.4 p.16
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw rough figures and label appropriately for four geometric statements: (a) OP and OQ meet at O; (b) XY and PQ intersect at M; (c) line l contains E and F but not D; (d) point P lies on AB.

time_bands.activity: Students press compass tips, pencil tips, and needle points onto paper and observe the marks. Through guided questioning — 'Does this dot have a size you can measure?' — the class arrives at the idea that a point is a precise location with no length, breadth, or height, and is named with a capital letter.

Each student folds a sheet of paper once and unfolds it; the crease is the line segment. Students label its two ends A and B and observe that AB is the shortest path between them. The class then discusses: if the crease were extended forever in both directions, what would it become? — arriving inductively at the concept of a line extending infinitely in both directions, denoted by two points or a lowercase letter, and the fact that any two points determine exactly one line.

Students work on Figure it Out Q4, section 2.4 p.16 ("Draw rough figures and label appropriately for four geometric statements....") in pairs, drawing rough sketches for each statement and labelling points, lines, and segments. Pairs compare sketches and discuss whether their diagrams correctly reflect each condition.

Whole-class consolidation: pairs share one sketch each; the class checks that segment notation (AB or BA), line notation (lowercase letter or two-point label), and point naming (capital letter) are used consistently. Common labelling errors are corrected aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse a line segment (finite, two endpoints) with a line (infinite, no endpoints); emphasise the arrow convention for lines during the sketch review. The paper-folding crease gives a vivid concrete referent that students can return to when the distinction blurs.

periods.activity_title: Rays All Around: Starting Points and Endless Directions

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.4 p.16
textbook_items_in_class.description: Name the rays shown in Fig. 2.5 (T, A, N, B) and determine whether T is the starting point of each ray.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 2.4 p.16
textbook_items_in_class.description: From Fig. 2.6 name: (a) five points; (b) a line; (c) four rays; (d) five line segments.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 2.4 p.17
textbook_items_in_class.description: Ray OA starts at O and passes through A and B. (a) Can it also be named OB? Why? (b) Can OA be written as AO? Why or why not?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.4 p.15
homework.description: Help Rihan (how many lines through one point?) and Sheetal (how many lines through two points?) find their answers.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.4 p.16
homework.description: Name the line segments in Fig. 2.4 (points L, M, P, Q, R); identify which of the five marked points lie on exactly one segment and which lie on two segments.

time_bands.activity: Students shine a torch at the wall in a darkened corner or imagine a sunbeam entering a window. Discussion: the light starts at a source and travels endlessly in one direction — this is a ray. Students articulate what distinguishes a ray from a line segment (one endpoint, extends infinitely one way) and from a line (extends infinitely both ways).

Students work on Figure it Out Q3, section 2.4 p.16 ("Name the rays shown in Fig. 2.5 (T, A, N, B) and determine whether T is the starting point of each ray.") individually, then compare with a partner. The class discusses the naming convention: the starting point is always written first.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q5, section 2.4 p.16 ("From Fig. 2.6 name: (a) five points; (b) a line; (c) four rays; (d) five line segments.") and Figure it Out Q6, section 2.4 p.17 ("Ray OA starts at O and passes through A and B...."), working in small groups. Groups share answers, with attention to Q6's discovery that a ray can be renamed using any point it passes through — as long as the starting point remains first.

Students draw one original figure in their notebooks containing at least one line, one ray, and one segment, labelling each with correct notation. Brief gallery walk: students check a neighbour's figure for correct notation and suggest corrections.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is writing the endpoint second when naming a ray — stress that the starting point is always the first letter in the ray's name, so OA and OB name the same ray but AO does not name any ray starting at O. Having established the distinction among points, segments, lines, and rays, students are now equipped to build the idea of an angle in the coming work.
materials: textbook open to Fig. 2.5 and Fig. 2.6

periods.activity_title: Two Rays, One Vertex: Naming and Identifying Angles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.5 p.19
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find angles in given pictures (bicycle, tiled pattern, ladder, bridge truss); draw the rays forming one angle and name its vertex.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.5 p.20
textbook_items_in_class.description: Explain why ∠APB (where three rays from P are shown) cannot be labelled as ∠P.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 2.5 p.20
textbook_items_in_class.description: Name the angles marked in the given figure (rays from T through P, R, Q).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 2.5 p.20
homework.description: Mark three non-collinear points A, B, C; draw all lines through pairs; count and name the lines; name and mark all angles using A, B, C.

time_bands.activity: Students open and close a pair of scissors slowly. The teacher asks: what stays fixed? (the pivot) What moves? (the blades, i.e., the two arms). Students identify the same structure in spectacles, a compass, and a hinged door. The class formulates: an angle is two rays sharing a common starting point called the vertex, and its size measures the rotation needed to move one arm onto the other.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 2.5 p.19 ("Find angles in given pictures (bicycle, tiled pattern, ladder, bridge truss)....") in pairs, sketching the two rays and marking the vertex for one angle in each picture. Pairs share their sketches with the group.

Whole class works through Figure it Out Q3, section 2.5 p.20 ("Explain why ∠APB...cannot be labelled as ∠P....") with teacher facilitation — the key insight is that the vertex letter alone is ambiguous when more than one angle shares that vertex. Students then attempt Figure it Out Q4, section 2.5 p.20 ("Name the angles marked in the given figure (rays from T through P, R, Q).") individually.

Students draw and label one angle of their own choice in their notebook, name it with three letters (vertex in the middle), and write one sentence explaining their naming. A few share aloud; the class confirms or corrects.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error is labelling an angle by its vertex letter alone when multiple angles share that vertex — Exercise Q3 is the ideal vehicle for addressing this directly. Watch for students who draw the arms as line segments rather than rays; redirect them to the definition and the scissors model where the arms extend beyond the pivot.
materials: scissors (one pair per pair of students)

periods.activity_title: How Many Lines, How Many Angles? Counting with Four Points

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.5 p.20
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw and label an angle with arms ST and SR.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 2.5 p.21
textbook_items_in_class.description: Mark four points A, B, C, D with no three collinear; draw all lines through pairs; count and name the lines; name and mark all angles using A, B, C, D.

time_bands.activity: Brief recall of angle notation using the arms-and-vertex language established while working on scissors and hinged objects. Students quickly draw one angle from memory, name it with three letters, and swap notebooks with a partner who checks the notation. Errors are corrected aloud.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q2, section 2.5 p.20 ("Draw and label an angle with arms ST and SR.") individually, making sure to draw rays (with arrows) and place the vertex letter correctly in the middle of the angle name.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q6, section 2.5 p.21 ("Mark four points A, B, C, D with no three collinear; draw all lines through pairs; count and name the lines; name and mark all angles....") working in pairs. They discover how many lines are possible (six) and systematically list all angles formed at each vertex by the crossing lines. Pairs compare their angle lists to catch omissions.

Quick whole-class share: how many distinct angles did pairs find? Students discuss whether changing the position of one point (while keeping no three collinear) changes the number of lines or the number of angles — establishing that the count depends on the number of points, not their specific positions.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes omit angles that appear at intersections of lines inside their figures — encourage them to mark each angle with a small arc as they name it, so none is skipped. Having worked systematically with four non-collinear points, students build the spatial sense needed for comparing angles in the next section.

periods.activity_title: Bigger or Smaller? Superimposition and the Circle Method

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.6 p.23
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fold a rectangular sheet to create angles; name and compare angles formed between the fold and the sides; make different angles by varied folding and identify the largest and smallest.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.6 p.23
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine which angle is greater in each case using the given figure (rays A, X, Y from O with B and C on base): (a) ∠AOB or ∠XOY; (b) ∠AOB or ∠XOB; (c) ∠XOB or ∠XOC. Discuss reasoning with friends.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.6 p.23
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which angle is greater: ∠XOY or ∠AOB (Fig. where arms of both angles are drawn from O)? Give reasons.

time_bands.activity: Students fold a rectangular sheet of paper into different angles, then try to compare two of their folds by overlapping them (superimposition): they align vertices and one arm, and observe which second arm extends further. The class formalises: when vertices and one arm coincide, the angle whose other arm is further from the shared arm is larger. The transparent-circle method is introduced as an alternative: draw a circle, place its centre at the vertex of each angle, and compare the arc intercepts.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 2.6 p.23 ("Fold a rectangular sheet to create angles; name and compare angles....") in pairs, using folding as a physical superimposition. They record which fold produces the largest angle and give a reason.

Students work through Figure it Out Q2, section 2.6 p.23 ("Determine which angle is greater in each case....") and Figure it Out Q3, section 2.6 p.23 ("Which angle is greater: ∠XOY or ∠AOB?....") using the textbook figure. For Q3, students write a reason: two angles with the same vertex but different arms — they reason about which arc intercept is larger without measuring numerically.

Class discussion: does the length of the arms affect which angle is larger? Students share their reasoning from the folding activity, arriving at the key insight that arm length does not determine angle size — only the amount of opening does.

periods.teacher_notes: A prevalent error is concluding that the angle with longer arms is larger — the folding activity and the slit-passing idea from section 2.7 together dismantle this misconception, so revisit arm-length independence whenever it surfaces here. The reasoning in Figure it Out Q3 is the key transition from visual comparison to justified argument.
materials: rectangular sheets of paper (two per student)
tracing paper or transparent sheet (one per pair)

periods.activity_title: Build, Arrange, and Challenge: The Rotating Arms Activity

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity 1, p.25
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students make 'rotating arms' using two paper straws inserted into the arms of a paper clip, create several rotating arms with different angles, arrange them from smallest to largest by superimposition, then perform the slit-passing challenge — tracing one rotating arm onto cardboard to make an angle-shaped slit and identifying which shuffled arm passes through it.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates making one rotating arm: two paper straws inserted into the two arms of a paper clip. Students each make three rotating arms, deliberately setting them to visually different angles — one clearly small, one medium, one large.

Students perform Activity 1, p.25 ("Students make 'rotating arms'...arrange them from smallest to largest by superimposition...."). Working in groups of four, they pool their arms (twelve angles) and arrange them in order from smallest to largest using superimposition, naming a winner for each comparison.

The slit-passing challenge from Activity 1, p.25: one student traces their rotating arm onto a card and cuts an angle-shaped slit; the remaining arms are shuffled and students predict which will pass through. Each prediction is tested and the result recorded. Students articulate why some arms pass (angle ≤ slit angle) and some do not — making explicit that arm length is irrelevant.

Groups share one surprising result from the slit challenge. The class discusses: if two rotating arms look very different in arm length but have the same opening, what happens? — consolidating the insight that angle size is purely about the amount of rotation, not arm length.

periods.teacher_notes: The slit-passing challenge is the physical proof that arm length does not affect angle size — ensure students articulate this in words before moving on, since the misconception is persistent. Watch for groups who compare arms by length rather than opening; redirect by asking them to slide one arm inside the other and look at the gap between second arms.
materials: card or thin cardboard (one piece per group)

periods.activity_title: Straight, Right, Acute, Obtuse: Folding into Definitions

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.8 p.29
textbook_items_in_class.description: Count right angles in classroom windows and identify other right angles in the classroom.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.8 p.30
textbook_items_in_class.description: On a dot grid, join A to other grid points to get a straight angle in all different ways.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.8 p.31
textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify acute, right, obtuse and straight angles in the previous figures shown in the chapter.

time_bands.activity: Students lay a sheet of paper flat and draw a straight line — the straight angle (180°, arms collinear, formed by a half-turn). They fold the paper exactly along that line: the fold bisects the straight angle. Students observe that both halves look identical, arriving at the definition of a right angle (90°). The class records: a straight angle contains exactly two right angles, and lines meeting at a right angle are perpendicular.

Students look around the classroom for right angles — Figure it Out Q1, section 2.8 p.29 ("Count right angles in classroom windows...."). They record their count and locations. Teacher introduces acute (less than 90°) and obtuse (between 90° and 180°) by opening and closing the folded paper to create angles smaller and larger than the right-angle crease.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2, section 2.8 p.30 ("On a dot grid, join A to other grid points to get a straight angle in all different ways.") — they discover multiple ways to make collinear points through A, establishing that a straight angle is not unique to horizontal orientation.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 2.8 p.31 ("Identify acute, right, obtuse and straight angles in the previous figures shown in the chapter."), scanning back through earlier chapter figures. A few examples are shared aloud and the class confirms the classification.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often believe a straight angle must be horizontal — the dot-grid exercise corrects this by requiring straight angles in multiple orientations. The paper-folding proof that bisecting a straight angle yields two equal right angles is more convincing than a statement; allow students to hold and compare both halves before declaring them equal.

periods.activity_title: Justifying Classifications and Spotting Patterns in Angle Counts

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.8 p.30
textbook_items_in_class.description: On a dot grid, join A to other grid points to get a right angle in all different ways (using the hint that line CAB must be bisected).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 2.8 p.31
textbook_items_in_class.description: Get a slanting crease on paper; fold to get a perpendicular crease. (a) How many right angles result? Justify they are exact right angles. (b) Describe the folding procedure so another person can replicate it.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.8 p.31
textbook_items_in_class.description: Explain why the words 'acute' (sharp) and 'obtuse' (blunt) have been chosen for these angle types.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 2.8 p.32
textbook_items_in_class.description: Count the number of acute angles in each of the three given triangle figures; predict the next figure and its acute angle count; identify the numerical pattern.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.8 p.31
homework.description: Make a few acute angles and a few obtuse angles; draw them in different orientations.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out Q3, section 2.8 p.30 ("On a dot grid, join A to other grid points to get a right angle in all different ways...."). They use the reasoning that a right angle is formed by bisecting a straight angle — so they first draw a straight angle through A and then find its midpoint direction. Pairs share how many distinct right-angle orientations they found.

Students carry out Figure it Out Q4, section 2.8 p.31 ("Get a slanting crease on paper; fold to get a perpendicular crease...."). They fold a slanting crease, then fold along it again to produce a perpendicular, count the four right angles formed, and write a justification using the bisection argument. Part (b) requires students to write step-by-step instructions for a classmate.

Brief class discussion on Figure it Out Q3, section 2.8 p.31 ("Explain why the words 'acute' (sharp) and 'obtuse' (blunt) have been chosen...."). Students reason from the everyday meanings of sharp and blunt to the geometric properties — acute angles resemble a sharp point, obtuse angles are broader and blunter.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q4, section 2.8 p.32 ("Count the number of acute angles in each of the three given triangle figures; predict the next figure...."). They count, record, and identify the pattern in the sequence of acute-angle counts, stating their conjecture in words.

periods.teacher_notes: The folding-to-perpendicular exercise is the chapter's clearest deductive moment: students must justify why the fold yields exact right angles, not just assert it — push for the bisection argument in their written answers. The acute-angle pattern task builds inductive reasoning that complements the deductive justification earlier in the unit.

periods.activity_title: Why 360°? Building the Degree System from a Full Turn

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 2.9 p.34
textbook_items_in_class.description: A circle divided into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, and 12 equal parts is shown; write the degree measure of each resulting angle near the indicated sector.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.9 p.35
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the unlabelled protractor diagram, write the measures of ∠KAL, ∠WAL, and ∠TAK by counting 1° units (and in groups of 5° or 10° using medium and large marks).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Think!, section 2.9 p.40
textbook_items_in_class.description: In Fig. 2.19, explain why ∠AOB = ∠BOC = ∠COD = ∠DOE = ∠EOF = ∠FOG = ∠GOH = ∠HOI (fill in the common value and justify).

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents: a full turn is divided into 360 equal parts, each called one degree (1°). The class reasons from first principles: straight angle = half turn = 180°; right angle = quarter turn = 90°. The historical note about Babylonian and ancient Indian roots is shared — the divisibility of 360 by many whole numbers makes it convenient. Students write these derivations in their notebooks.

Students work on Figure it Out, section 2.9 p.34 ("A circle divided into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, and 12 equal parts...."). For each division they compute 360 ÷ (number of parts) to find the degree measure of each sector. They check: does 12 equal parts give 30°? Does 6 give 60°? The deductive chain from 360° is explicit.

Students read Figure it Out Q1, section 2.9 p.35 ("Using the unlabelled protractor diagram, write the measures of ∠KAL, ∠WAL, and ∠TAK....") by counting 1° units and grouping into 5° and 10° spans. Teacher introduces the dual-scale protractor and explains why two scales exist — reading from left or right depending on which arm aligns with 0°.

Students attempt Think!, section 2.9 p.40 ("In Fig. 2.19, explain why all consecutive angles are equal....") in pairs, reasoning that a full rotation divided into equal parts gives each equal share — a deductive justification, not just an observation.

periods.teacher_notes: The most frequent protractor error at this stage is reading from the wrong scale — the dual-scale introduction is the place to make this explicit; ask students to state aloud which arm is at 0° before reading any angle. The divisibility discussion around 360 builds genuine number sense alongside the geometry.
materials: printed or drawn circle divided into equal parts (teacher-prepared on board)
textbook open to section 2.9 p.34–35 and p.40

periods.activity_title: Reading the Protractor: Labelled Scales and Derived Measures

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 2.9 p.36
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the labelled protractor figure (rays O, P, Q, R, S, T, U), name all different angles and write their degree measures; determine which scale (inner or outer) to use and apply subtraction where needed.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Mind the Mistake, section 2.9 p.44
textbook_items_in_class.description: Six protractor-reading figures (∠U, ∠V, ∠W, ∠X, ∠Y, ∠Z) show incorrect student usage; identify the error(s) in each and explain how the correct reading should be made.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 2.9 p.41
homework.description: Measure and write the degree measures for six angles (a–f) drawn in varied orientations.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out, section 2.9 p.36 ("Using the labelled protractor figure (rays O, P, Q, R, S, T, U)...."). For each angle, they identify which scale to read and, where a ray does not fall on 0°, apply subtraction to find the measure. The teacher circulates and questions students on their scale choice before they record any number.

Students tackle Mind the Mistake, section 2.9 p.44 ("Six protractor-reading figures...show incorrect student usage; identify the error(s)...."). Working in pairs, they diagnose each error — misaligned centre, wrong scale, base arm not at 0° — and write one sentence of correction per figure. Pairs swap and critique each other's diagnoses.

Whole-class debrief: teacher selects three of the six 'Mind the Mistake' figures and asks different pairs to explain the error. The class votes on whether each diagnosis is complete. The session closes with students stating the three-step reading rule: align centre at vertex, align base arm at 0°, read the scale the base arm starts from.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established the dual-scale logic in the previous unit, this unit applies it under deliberate error conditions — Mind the Mistake is the chapter's most powerful self-correction tool, so give it adequate time. Students who finish the labelled protractor exercise early can be directed to Figure it Out Q6, section 2.9 p.42 as extension.
materials: textbook open to section 2.9 p.36 and p.44

periods.activity_title: Make Your Own Protractor: Folding Degrees into Paper

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity 2, p.37
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students make their own protractor by successive paper folding: cut a circle, fold to semicircle (180°), fold again to quarter-circle (90°), fold again to mark 45° and 135°, fold once more to mark 22.5° and 67.5° etc., then unfold and label all creases, identifying angle bisectors and reading off the resulting degree measures.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.9 p.40
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the degree measures of three sets of angles drawn in the figures using the handmade protractor: ∠IHJ (figure 1), ∠GHK (figure 2), ∠IHJ (figure 3).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.9 p.40
homework.description: Find the degree measures of different angles in the classroom using the handmade protractor.

time_bands.activity: Students carry out Activity 2, p.37 ("Students make their own protractor by successive paper folding...."). Each student cuts a circle from paper, folds to a semicircle (labelling 180°), folds to a quarter-circle (labelling 90°), then to 45°/135°, then to 22.5°/67.5°. After unfolding, they draw lines on the creases and label all degree marks, identifying each crease as an angle bisector of the angle on either side of it.

Students use their handmade protractors to solve Figure it Out Q1, section 2.9 p.40 ("Find the degree measures of three sets of angles...."). They align the handmade protractor's centre and 0° line with each given angle and read off the nearest labelled crease. Students note the precision limitation of the handmade tool.

Brief class discussion: why does the handmade protractor only mark certain degree values? Students reason from the halving process (180 → 90 → 45 → 22.5) and identify which angles cannot be read exactly. The concept of angle bisector is named explicitly for each crease.

periods.teacher_notes: Each student must bring or be supplied a circular cut-out at the start — pre-cut circles save significant time. Watch for students who fold imprecisely; an off-centre fold produces an asymmetric protractor and incorrect readings, so demonstrate one clean fold before students begin.
materials: circular paper cut-outs (one per student, radius ~8 cm)
textbook open to Activity 2 p.37 and Figure it Out Q1 p.40

periods.activity_title: Reflex Angles, Clock Angles, and Real-World Turns

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 2.9 p.41
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine how to find the degree measure of a reflex angle (greater than 180°) using a protractor.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.9 p.45
textbook_items_in_class.description: Angles in a clock: (a) explain why the angle at 1 o'clock is 30°; (b) find angles at 2, 4, and 6 o'clock; (c) explore other clock angles.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.9 p.45
textbook_items_in_class.description: Express the opening of a door as an angle; identify the vertex and arms.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 2.9 p.42
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the protractor figure with rays A, B, C from X along base E, find the degree measures of ∠BXE, ∠CXE, ∠AXB, and ∠BXC.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 2.9 p.42
homework.description: Find the degree measures of ∠PQR, ∠PQS, and ∠PQT from the given figure with multiple rays from Q.

time_bands.activity: Students tackle Figure it Out Q4, section 2.9 p.41 ("Determine how to find the degree measure of a reflex angle....") in pairs. They reason: since the protractor only reads up to 180°, a reflex angle (> 180°) must be measured by reading its non-reflex partner and subtracting from 360°. Pairs share their reasoning.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 2.9 p.45 ("Angles in a clock: (a) explain why the angle at 1 o'clock is 30°...."). They reason that 360° ÷ 12 = 30° per hour-mark, so 1 o'clock = 30°, 2 o'clock = 60°, 4 o'clock = 120°, 6 o'clock = 180°. Part (c) invites exploration of other clock positions.

Students solve Figure it Out Q6, section 2.9 p.42 ("find the degree measures of ∠BXE, ∠CXE, ∠AXB, and ∠BXC....") using the protractor and applying subtraction where a ray does not start at 0°. Figure it Out Q2, section 2.9 p.45 ("Express the opening of a door as an angle....") is attempted: students identify the hinge as vertex, the door frame and door edge as arms.

Quick group challenge: each group writes one real-life angle scenario (swing, gate, window) and identifies the vertex and two arms in words. Groups share; the class checks that vertex and arm definitions are correctly applied.

periods.teacher_notes: The reflex angle strategy (360° minus the non-reflex partner) is the key new reasoning move here — ensure students write the subtraction explicitly rather than reading a number off a ruler. The clock context is an excellent bridge between the degree system and everyday experience.
materials: a classroom clock or clock-face drawing on the board

periods.activity_title: Draw Any Angle: Four Steps, Two Games, Perfect Aim

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Let's Play a Game #1, section 2.10 p.48
textbook_items_in_class.description: Team game: one team secretly draws an angle with a protractor; the other team visually estimates the measure; score is the absolute difference in degrees. Each team gets five turns; lowest score wins.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Let's Play a Game #2, section 2.10 p.48
textbook_items_in_class.description: Team game: one team announces a degree measure; a player from the other team draws it freehand on the board (teammates guide verbally); score is the absolute difference between drawn and intended angle. Five turns each.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.10 p.50
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use a protractor to draw angles of 110°, 40°, 75°, 112°, and 134°.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.10 p.50
homework.description: Draw an angle whose measure equals the given angle (∠HIJ); write the steps followed.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the four explicit steps to draw 30° (∠TIN): (1) draw the base ray IT; (2) place the protractor centre on I, aligning the base ray to 0°; (3) locate the 30° mark and make a point; (4) join I to that point with a ruler to form the second arm. Students copy the steps and draw 30° themselves, then check by re-measuring.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2, section 2.10 p.50 ("Use a protractor to draw angles of 110°, 40°, 75°, 112°, and 134°.") individually. For each angle they label the vertex and both arms. A partner checks by measuring the drawn angle with their own protractor.

The class plays Let's Play a Game #1, section 2.10 p.48 ("one team secretly draws an angle; the other team visually estimates the measure; score is absolute difference....") and Let's Play a Game #2, section 2.10 p.48 ("one team announces a degree; a player draws it freehand; teammates guide verbally...."). Two rounds of each game are played.

Debrief: which angles were hardest to estimate and hardest to draw freehand? Students identify angles close to 45°, 90°, or 135° as easiest anchors. The four-step drawing procedure is restated from memory by one student.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently draw the angle on the wrong side of the base ray when the required measure is obtuse — insist on a quick sketch estimate before placing the protractor so students know which side the angle should open. The team games build estimation skill and make the degree scale intuitive through playful repetition.
materials: blackboard and chalk or whiteboard and marker for team games

periods.activity_title: Guess, Measure, Record: Figure 2.23 Angle Survey

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.10 p.49
textbook_items_in_class.description: In Fig. 2.23, list all possible angles; guess their measures; measure with a protractor; record guesses vs. actual in a table.

time_bands.activity: Students examine Fig. 2.23 and, without a protractor, list every distinct angle they can identify in the figure, marking each with a small arc. They write their guesses for each angle measure in a table with columns: Angle Name | Guess | Actual.

Students measure each listed angle from Figure it Out Q1, section 2.10 p.49 ("In Fig. 2.23, list all possible angles; guess their measures; measure with a protractor; record guesses vs. actual in a table.") with a protractor, filling in the Actual column. They compute the absolute difference between guess and actual for each angle and circle the angle where their guess was furthest off.

In groups of four, students compare their tables — which angles were most consistently misjudged? Groups identify whether they tended to underestimate or overestimate and formulate one strategy to improve their next estimate.

Whole-class share: one group presents their improvement strategy. The class votes on the most useful tip. The teacher notes that estimation skill comes from repeated deliberate practice, not from one exercise alone.

periods.teacher_notes: Some students will rush the guessing phase and write estimates after measuring — insist that the Guess column is filled before the protractor is picked up, and circulate to enforce this. The self-reflective comparison of guess vs. actual builds metacognitive awareness of angle-estimation bias, which is as valuable as the measuring skill itself.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.11 p.52
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use a protractor to find the measures of ∠PTR, ∠PTQ, ∠PTW, and ∠WTP from the given figure; classify each as acute, obtuse, right, or reflex.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Let's Explore, section 2.11 p.53
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given ∠TER = 80° in a figure where ∠REB is a straight angle and ∠SET is perpendicular context, find the measures of ∠BET and ∠SET.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the complete classification on the board: acute (0°–90°), right (90°), obtuse (90°–180°), straight (180°), reflex (180°–360°). Students copy and write one numeric example for each type from memory.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 2.11 p.51 ("On dot grids, join A to other grid points to get (a) an acute angle, (b) an obtuse angle, (c) a reflex angle; mark the intended angles with curves.") individually. They must mark the arc on the correct side to show the intended angle — a key distinction for reflex angles.

Students measure and classify angles in Figure it Out Q2, section 2.11 p.52 ("find the measures of ∠PTR, ∠PTQ, ∠PTW, and ∠WTP...."), using the protractor correctly for each orientation and applying the 360° − non-reflex method for ∠WTP if it is reflex.

Students attempt Let's Explore, section 2.11 p.53 ("Given ∠TER = 80°...find the measures of ∠BET and ∠SET.") reasoning from the straight-angle property (∠TER + ∠BET = 180°) and the perpendicular property to derive both unknown measures without measuring.

periods.teacher_notes: The reflex angle arc direction is the most common error in Q1 — if the arc curves the wrong way, the drawn angle becomes acute even though the student intended reflex; insist on the arc always being drawn on the side of the intended region. Let's Explore is the chapter's first angle-sum reasoning task and rewards students who can apply the straight-angle definition deductively.

homework.description: Make any figure that contains three acute angles, one right angle, and two obtuse angles.

time_bands.activity: Students draw angles of 140°, 82°, 195°, 70°, and 35° from Figure it Out Q1, section 2.11 p.53 ("Draw angles of 140°, 82°, 195°, 70°, and 35° using a protractor.") — the 195° angle requires the reflex strategy (draw 360° − 195° = 165° and mark the reflex side). Students label and classify each drawn angle.

Students estimate and then measure the six angles in Figure it Out Q2, section 2.11 p.53 ("Estimate the size of each of six given angles (a–f) and then measure...."), recording guesses first. Each angle is classified as acute, right, obtuse, or reflex after measuring.

Students solve Figure it Out Q6, section 2.11 p.54 ("The Ashoka Chakra has 24 spokes....") by computing 360° ÷ 24 = 15° per adjacent spoke, then find the largest acute angle formed between non-adjacent spokes (the largest multiple of 15° that is still less than 90°, i.e., 75°).

Students work on Figure it Out Q7, section 2.11 p.54 ("Puzzle: find all acute angle measures such that double, triple, and quadruple are still acute, but five times is obtuse."). They reason: 4x < 90° and 5x > 90°, so 18° < x < 22.5°. Students list whole-number solutions (19°, 20°, 21°, 22°) and verify each.

periods.teacher_notes: Drawing 195° is the first time students must explicitly use the reflex drawing strategy — ensure they draw the 165° angle first and then indicate the reflex region with an arc, rather than attempting to read 195° directly off the protractor. The Ashoka Chakra problem is an elegant real-world application and rewards students who connect divisibility of 360 to the angle system introduced in section 2.9.

items.prompt: Which of the following best describes a point in geometry?

options.label: A
options.text: A dot whose size depends on the pencil used to draw it

options.label: B
options.text: A flat region bounded by straight edges

options.label: C
options.text: A precise location with no length, breadth, or height

options.label: D
options.text: A short path connecting two locations on a surface

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A point is a precise location with no length, breadth, or height.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the definition of a point as a dimensionless location, modelled by a compass tip or needle point.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is conflating a point with a line segment — confusing a location with a path.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is confusing a point with a plane region or polygon.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student believes the visible dot drawn on paper is the point itself, not understanding that the drawn mark is only a representation.

inclusivity.support: Let the student re-read the opening paragraph of section 2.1 and list three real-life models of a point before answering.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain in their own words why a dot drawn with a pencil is not truly a geometric point, and what the difference is.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 2.4 p.16
exercise.description: Draw rough figures and label appropriately for four geometric statements: (a) OP and OQ meet at O; (b) XY and PQ intersect at M; (c) line l contains E and F but not D; (d) point P lies on AB.

items.prompt: Ray OA starts at O and passes through A. Which statement about this ray is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The ray can also be named OB if B is another point on it beyond A, because the starting point O remains first

options.label: B
options.text: The ray can be written as AO because the two endpoint letters can be swapped

options.label: C
options.text: The ray extends infinitely in both directions from O

options.label: D
options.text: The ray has a definite length equal to the distance OA

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The ray can also be named OB if B lies on it beyond A, because the starting point O must always appear first in the name.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the ray-naming convention: starting point first, followed by any other point the ray passes through.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student believes a ray's name can be reversed like a line segment's name, ignoring the directional nature of a ray.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is confusing a ray with a line segment, which has a fixed finite length.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is confusing a ray with a line, which extends infinitely in both directions.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to draw ray OA with an arrow, mark another point B beyond A, then write two names for the ray — they should see O comes first in both.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain why AO cannot name a ray starting at O, and what geometric object AO would describe instead.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.4 p.16
exercise.description: Name the rays shown in Fig. 2.5 (T, A, N, B) and determine whether T is the starting point of each ray.

items.prompt: Three rays share the same starting point P: ray PA, ray PB, and ray PC. A student labels one of the angles as ∠P. Why is this labelling incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: The label ∠P is ambiguous because there are multiple angles at vertex P

options.label: B
options.text: The label ∠P is wrong because angles must be labelled with numbers, not letters

options.label: C
options.text: The label ∠P is wrong because P is not the vertex of any angle here

options.label: D
options.text: The label ∠P is wrong because the vertex letter must be written last, not first

teacher_guide.expected_answer: ∠P is ambiguous when multiple angles share vertex P; each angle must be named with three letters, placing the vertex letter in the middle, such as ∠APB or ∠BPC.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the three-letter angle-naming rule: one letter from each arm and the vertex letter in the middle.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has not understood that P is the vertex; they may be confusing the starting point with the vertex.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has invented an incorrect rule about letter order, possibly reversing the correct convention.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has generalised from some other labelling context and believes numerical labels are mandatory.

inclusivity.support: Let the student re-read section 2.5 on angle naming and find one example where three-letter notation removes ambiguity.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to draw a figure with four rays from one point and write all distinct angle names possible, explaining why ∠P alone would not work.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.5 p.19
exercise.description: Find angles in given pictures (bicycle, tiled pattern, ladder, bridge truss); draw the rays forming one angle and name its vertex.

items.prompt: Draw an angle with arms ST and SR. Name the angle using three letters, placing the vertex letter in the middle. Write the name of the vertex.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The angle is ∠TSR (or equivalently ∠RST). The vertex is S, since S is the common starting point of both rays ST and SR.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the shared starting point of the two rays as the vertex and write the three-letter name with the vertex in the middle.

inclusivity.support: Prompt the student to place a dot at the starting point of each ray and ask which dot appears twice — that is the vertex.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write one more valid name for the same angle and explain why both names are correct.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.5 p.20
exercise.description: Draw and label an angle with arms ST and SR.

items.prompt: A straight angle is bisected by a ray from its vertex. What type of angle is each half, and what is its measure?

options.label: A
options.text: Each half is a right angle measuring 90°

options.label: B
options.text: Each half is a straight angle measuring 180°

options.label: C
options.text: Each half is an acute angle measuring 45°

options.label: D
options.text: Each half is an obtuse angle measuring 120°

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each half is a right angle measuring 90°, because bisecting a straight angle (180°) gives two equal parts each of 180° ÷ 2 = 90°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the definition: bisecting a straight angle (180°) yields two equal right angles (90° each).

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student halved 90° instead of 180°, suggesting they confused the right angle with the straight angle as the starting value.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student did not apply the bisection — they believe the halves are the same type as the whole.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student used an incorrect value (possibly 240° ÷ 2) or guessed without applying the definition.

inclusivity.support: Let the student fold a straight-angle piece of paper in half and measure one half with a set-square to confirm 90°.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain, using the definition of a right angle, why two right angles always combine to form a straight angle.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.8 p.29
exercise.description: Count right angles in classroom windows and identify other right angles in the classroom.

items.prompt: A dot-grid figure shows a straight angle at point A formed by points C, A, and B all on the same line. A student draws ray AE such that ∠CAE = ∠EAB. What type of angle is ∠CAE?

options.label: A
options.text: Acute angle

options.label: B
options.text: Obtuse angle

options.label: C
options.text: Right angle

options.label: D
options.text: Straight angle

teacher_guide.expected_answer: ∠CAE is a right angle. Since C, A, B are collinear, ∠CAB = 180°. Ray AE bisects it, so ∠CAE = ∠EAB = 90°, which is a right angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the bisection property: a ray that bisects a straight angle creates two right angles of 90° each.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have thought the bisecting ray creates a small angle rather than applying the 180° ÷ 2 calculation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have estimated visually without using the bisection property.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confused the original straight angle with one of its halves.

inclusivity.support: Have the student mark the 180° of the straight angle and then divide it by 2 before classifying the result.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to draw a different straight angle through A on the dot grid and find a different ray that bisects it, then name the resulting right angle.

exercise.description: On a dot grid, join A to other grid points to get a right angle in all different ways (using the hint that line CAB must be bisected).

items.section_title: Types of Angles and their Measures
items.prompt: An angle measures 215°. Which type of angle is it?

options.label: A
options.text: Acute angle

options.label: B
options.text: Obtuse angle

options.label: C
options.text: Reflex angle

options.label: D
options.text: Straight angle

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 215° is a reflex angle because it lies in the range 180° to 360°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the classification: reflex angles have measures strictly between 180° and 360°.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student applied the obtuse range (90°–180°) incorrectly, possibly misreading 215° as a two-digit number.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confused 215° with 180°, not distinguishing the boundary from the interior of the range.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student applied the acute range (0°–90°) and likely estimated without checking the given value.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to write the five angle types in order of increasing measure with their degree ranges before answering.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find the non-reflex angle that pairs with 215° to make a full turn and name its type.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.11 p.51
exercise.description: On dot grids, join A to other grid points to get (a) an acute angle, (b) an obtuse angle, (c) a reflex angle; mark the intended angles with curves.

items.section_title: Types of Angles and their Measures
items.prompt: To draw a reflex angle of 195° using a protractor, a student must first draw its non-reflex partner and then mark the reflex region. What is the measure of the non-reflex partner angle?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the reflex angle from 360° to find the non-reflex partner: 360° − 195° = 165°.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student subtracted from 180° instead of 360°, confusing the straight angle with the full turn.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student subtracted 195° from 210° or used 180° − 165° in reverse, making an arithmetic error.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added 195° and 150° or reversed the subtraction, finding a value larger than 180°.

inclusivity.support: Remind the student that a full turn is 360°, then ask them to compute 360° − 195° step by step.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to classify the non-reflex partner angle (165°) and explain whether it is acute, obtuse, right, or straight.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.11 p.53
exercise.description: Draw angles of 140°, 82°, 195°, 70°, and 35° using a protractor.

items.prompt: Two angles, ∠PQR and ∠XYZ, are drawn on separate sheets. A student places one angle on top of the other, aligning their vertices and one arm. The second arm of ∠PQR extends beyond the second arm of ∠XYZ. Which angle is greater? Explain your reasoning using the superimposition method.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: ∠PQR is greater. When vertices and one arm coincide, the angle whose second arm lies further from the shared arm is larger. Since ∠PQR's second arm extends beyond ∠XYZ's second arm, ∠PQR requires more rotation to reach its second arm and is therefore greater.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the superimposition method: the angle whose free arm lies further from the shared arm is the larger angle.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to physically fold two paper angles and overlay them, describing in words which arm sticks out further.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain what would happen if arm lengths were different but the opening was the same — which angle would the superimposition method declare larger?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.6 p.23
exercise.description: Fold a rectangular sheet to create angles; name and compare angles formed between the fold and the sides; make different angles by varied folding and identify the largest and smallest.

items.prompt: A student makes a slanting crease on a sheet of paper. She then folds the paper along that crease so that the two halves of the crease coincide exactly. She claims that the new fold is perpendicular to the original crease and that four right angles are formed. Justify her claim using the paper-folding argument from the chapter.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: When the paper is folded so that the two halves of the slanting crease lie on top of each other, the new fold bisects the straight angle (180°) on each side of the original crease. Since bisecting 180° gives two equal parts of 90° each, each of the four angles formed at the intersection is exactly 90° — a right angle. Lines meeting at right angles are perpendicular, so the new fold is perpendicular to the original crease.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the bisection argument: folding along the crease so both halves coincide bisects the 180° straight angle, yielding two right angles of 90° each on each side, giving four right angles in total.

inclusivity.support: Have the student try the fold physically and count the right-angle corners formed, then connect each to the 180° ÷ 2 = 90° calculation.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write step-by-step instructions for a classmate to replicate the fold and identify each of the four right angles by name.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 2.8 p.31
exercise.description: Get a slanting crease on paper; fold to get a perpendicular crease. (a) How many right angles result? Justify they are exact right angles. (b) Describe the folding procedure so another person can replicate it.

items.prompt: A circle is divided into 9 equal parts by 9 rays from its centre. What is the degree measure of each equal sector? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each sector measures 40°. Working: a full turn = 360°. Dividing equally into 9 parts gives 360° ÷ 9 = 40° per sector.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the full-turn measure of 360° by the number of equal parts: 360° ÷ 9 = 40°.

inclusivity.support: Remind the student that a full turn equals 360° and ask them to write the division before computing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find the smallest number of equal parts into which 360° can be divided so that each sector is an acute angle, and justify the answer.

exercise.description: A circle divided into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, and 12 equal parts is shown; write the degree measure of each resulting angle near the indicated sector.

items.prompt: A labelled protractor shows ray M aligned with the 0° mark on the outer scale and ray N pointing to 65° on the outer scale. A student reads the inner scale instead and records the angle as 115°. Identify the error and explain how the correct measure should be read.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student read from the wrong (inner) scale. Since ray M is aligned to 0° on the outer scale, the reading must be taken from the outer scale. Ray N points to 65° on the outer scale, so the correct measure of the angle is 65°. The inner scale reads the supplement of the outer scale at each position — 180° − 65° = 115° — which is the value the student incorrectly recorded.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the dual-scale rule: always read from the scale on which the base arm aligns to 0°.

inclusivity.support: Tell the student to first find the 0° end that the base ray touches, and then trace along only that scale to the second ray.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain why the two scales at any given mark always sum to 180°, and how this is connected to the supplementary angle relationship.

exercise.description: Using the labelled protractor figure (rays O, P, Q, R, S, T, U), name all different angles and write their degree measures; determine which scale (inner or outer) to use and apply subtraction where needed.

items.prompt: Riya makes three rotating arms with the same length straws but different openings: one small, one medium, one large. She cuts an angle-shaped slit in cardboard by tracing the medium arm. She then shuffles all three arms and tries to pass each through the slit. Which arm(s) will pass through, and which will not? Explain your answer in terms of what determines whether an arm passes through.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The small and medium arms will pass through the slit; the large arm will not. Whether an arm passes through depends solely on the size of its opening (angle), not the length of its straws. Any arm whose angle is less than or equal to the slit's angle fits; the large arm's wider opening means it cannot enter without bending.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the principle that angle size is determined by the amount of opening, not arm length — an arm passes the slit only if its angle does not exceed the slit's angle.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to imagine sliding the small arm into the slit opening — would it have enough room? Then try the large arm.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to predict what would happen if Riya used a different set of straws (longer or shorter) to make a new medium arm with the same angle — would it pass through the original slit?

exercise.description: Students make 'rotating arms' using two paper straws inserted into the arms of a paper clip, create several rotating arms with different angles, arrange them from smallest to largest by superimposition, then perform the slit-passing challenge — tracing one rotating arm onto cardboard to make an angle-shaped slit and identifying which shuffled arm passes through it.

items.prompt: A student folds a circular paper disc in half to get a semicircle (180°), then folds again to get a quarter-circle (90°), then folds once more. What angle does each section of the final fold represent? How many distinct crease lines does the fully unfolded disc have, and what degree measure does each crease mark?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: After three folds, each section represents 180° ÷ 2 ÷ 2 ÷ 2 = 22.5°. The fully unfolded disc has 3 crease lines (from the three folds). These creases mark 45°, 90°, and 135° (and their supplementary partners on the other side of the diameter), with the smallest sector being 45° and 22.5° depending on interpretation. Precisely: fold 1 creates 1 crease at 180°; fold 2 creates 1 crease at 90° (and 270° on the full circle); fold 3 creates creases at 45° and 135°. So the three distinct crease lines mark 45°, 90°, and 135° above the base diameter.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply successive halving: each fold halves the previous angle; track cumulative creases at 180°, 90°, 45°, and 135°.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to fold a physical circle three times and unfold it, counting the creases and measuring one angle with a protractor.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to predict what the crease angles would be after a fourth fold and explain how many distinct crease lines would appear in total.

exercise.description: Students make their own protractor by successive paper folding: cut a circle, fold to semicircle (180°), fold again to quarter-circle (90°), fold again to mark 45° and 135°, fold once more to mark 22.5° and 67.5° etc., then unfold and label all creases, identifying angle bisectors and reading off the resulting degree measures.

items.prompt: An angle drawn in a figure measures 250° when taken on the reflex side. Using a standard protractor (which reads only up to 180°), explain the strategy to measure this reflex angle, and find what the protractor would directly show for the non-reflex part.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The protractor reads only up to 180°, so the reflex angle (250°) cannot be read directly. The strategy is to measure the non-reflex angle on the other side: non-reflex = 360° − 250° = 110°. The protractor would directly show 110°. The reflex angle is then 360° − 110° = 250°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the reflex angle from 360° to find the non-reflex partner, read the non-reflex partner with the protractor, then subtract from 360° to verify.

inclusivity.support: Remind the student that reflex and non-reflex angles at the same vertex together make a full turn of 360°, then ask them to set up the equation.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find two different reflex angles whose non-reflex partners are both acute, and state the range of reflex angles for which the non-reflex partner is acute.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 2.9 p.41
exercise.description: Determine how to find the degree measure of a reflex angle (greater than 180°) using a protractor.

items.prompt: A team in a game secretly draws an angle and a student estimates it to be 70°. The actual angle is 83°. What is the student's score for this turn? If the student's scores for five turns are 13, 7, 20, 5, and 11, what is the team's total score?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Score for this turn = |70° − 83°| = |−13°| = 13. Total score for five turns = 13 + 7 + 20 + 5 + 11 = 56.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the absolute difference between estimated and actual angle for each turn, then sum all five turn scores.

inclusivity.support: Write out |estimated − actual| for the first turn explicitly and ask the student to repeat the same calculation for the remaining turns.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find a set of five estimates (different from the given ones) that would give a total score of exactly 20, if the actual angles are 45°, 90°, 60°, 30°, and 120°.

exercise.book_ref: Let's Play a Game #1, section 2.10 p.48
exercise.description: Team game: one team secretly draws an angle with a protractor; the other team visually estimates the measure; score is the absolute difference in degrees. Each team gets five turns; lowest score wins.

items.prompt: A figure contains three rays from one point. A student lists the following angles from the figure and guesses their measures: ∠1 = 40°, ∠2 = 75°, ∠3 = 110°. After measuring, the actual values are: ∠1 = 35°, ∠2 = 80°, ∠3 = 105°. Compute the absolute difference between guess and actual for each angle, and find the total estimation error.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the absolute difference between each guessed and actual angle measure, then sum the three differences.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to fill in a table with columns Angle | Guess | Actual | |Guess − Actual| for each angle, then add the last column.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to redesign their guesses so that the total estimation error is at most 10°, given the same actual angles.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.10 p.49
exercise.description: In Fig. 2.23, list all possible angles; guess their measures; measure with a protractor; record guesses vs. actual in a table.
